title: Global sign patterns of ES solutions vs local predictions (Legendre symbols of x, y, z mod small primes)
connection: For each global solution record (x/ℓ), (y/ℓ), (z/ℓ). If some locally allowed pattern never occurs globally at hard primes, that is a hidden global constraint (reciprocity-type).
why: Hidden global constraints are exactly what T1 is; finding more of them maps the obstruction landscape.
first_step: Using existing solution data for p ≤ 10^6, tabulate patterns at ℓ = 3, 5, 7 and test against local frequencies.

title: Lipschitz/Hurwitz quaternions with integer coefficients ≥ 0 as cone (semiring N[i,j,k])
connection: The semiring of quaternions with non-negative coefficients is multiplicatively closed? (No: i·i = −1 ∉.) Hence a natural non-commutative cone must be designed (e.g. positive real part + norm conditions).
why: Recording a failed cone design avoids wasted searches and clarifies minimal axioms (multiplicative closure is essential for Lemma 3.1).
first_step: List candidate quaternionic cones and check multiplicative closure; keep only valid ones for a search.

title: ES in rings of integers of CM fields with cone from the maximal real subfield
connection: For a CM field K with totally real K⁺, use denominators in K whose relative norm to K⁺ is totally positive. Units of K⁺ (rank ≥ 1 when [K⁺:Q] ≥ 2) make the unit mechanism available.
why: Another family where infinite units collapse ES; confirms that only Q and imaginary quadratic K (unit rank 0) are hard.
first_step: For Q(ζ_8), test the unit mechanism with units of Q(√2).

title: ES over Z[i] for Gaussian primes in the sector cone: does the T1 square obstruction appear at Gaussian squares?
connection: If a Gaussian analogue of certificate lines exists, T1 predicts emptiness at Gaussian squares π² with suitable congruence. Test whether Gaussian squares are the hardest Gaussian-cone cases.
why: A T1 analogue in Z[i] would show T1 is about quadratic reciprocity in general number fields (quartic reciprocity may refine it).
first_step: Classify Gaussian-cone solutions by type and check emptiness of 'line' families at π² for small π.

title: Positive ES in Q(√−1) with the cone 'Re > 0 and Im ≥ 0' (half-closed quadrant) vs both-sign cones
connection: Bradford–Ionascu's cone is Re, Im of equal sign; a strict first quadrant is multiplicatively closed only up to 90° sums (it is not closed: i·i). Clarify which quadrant-like sets are closed and which make ES non-trivial.
why: Cone design determines the world; misdesigned cones give trivial or empty problems.
first_step: Check closure of the equal-sign cone (product of two first-quadrant elements can leave the quadrant) — note Bradford–Ionascu's cone may not be multiplicatively closed, and record what they actually require.

title: ES for elements of Z_p (p-adic) with 'positivity' from an embedding into R — not well-defined
connection: Category-error check: Z_p has no archimedean embedding, so positivity cannot be imported; the meaningful p-adic analogues are local solubility (always) and p-adic cones (items in batch B).
why: Record the closed item to avoid repeated consideration.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Harmonic numbers' p-adic valuations (Boyd) and the integrality of Σ 1/x
connection: Boyd's conjecture: J_p = {n : p | numerator(H_n)} is finite; studied via p-adic trees. ES at p is a p-adic statement about which unit-fraction sums have valuation −1 at p.
why: p-adic tree methods for harmonic sums might organize ES solutions by p-adic structure (Type I/II = which denominators carry p).
first_step: Low priority; read Boyd's 'A p-adic study of the partial sums of the harmonic series' for tree technique.

title: Waring-type 'every n is a sum of three triangular numbers' (Gauss) ↔ ES via genus theory
connection: Gauss's Eureka theorem follows from three squares. Problems equivalent to ternary quadratic representability are 'easy'; ES's equation 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is cubic. A quadratic slice (fixing one variable) gives binary problems.
why: Fixing x gives the 2-term problem, whose solvability is a binary-form/divisor question; the union over x is ES. Genus theory over the union is the conceptual gap.
first_step: Context; check whether 'union over x of binary-form problems' has a ternary-form encoding (cf. Borwein–Choi item).

title: Real cyclotomic field Q(ζ_p)^+: cyclotomic units tied to p supply ES solutions; descend by trace
connection: Q(ζ_p)^+ has totally positive cyclotomic units (e.g. squares of (1 − ζ^a)/(1 − ζ) suitably normalized) and p is totally ramified. Positive ES for 4/p holds there by the unit mechanism; tracing a solution down to Q gives 2(p − 1)/p = Σ Tr(1/α_i), an Egyptian-type identity with trace numerators.
why: Provides an explicit p-indexed family of algebraic solutions whose descent might be engineered (choice of unit) to have unit-fraction traces — an algebraic source of p-dependent certificates.
first_step: For p = 5, 13, 17 compute a totally positive cyclotomic unit η ≡ −1 mod an inert-type prime and the resulting solution; compute traces of the denominators.

title: Repeated denominators never occur for p ≡ 1 (mod 4): explains 'distinct is WLOG'
connection: The data (499/499 primes) show no solution with x = y or y = z. Proof sketch: x = y gives z = px/(2(2x − p)); gcd(2x − p, x) | p forces 2x − p ∈ {1, p}, and 2x − p = 1 needs x = (p+1)/2 even, i.e. p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Similar for y = z.
why: A clean lemma removing a case and showing the 'repeat world' is empty exactly in the hard class — another archimedean/2-adic coincidence.
first_step: Write out both cases (x = y, y = z) carefully and record the lemma.

title: ES over the ring Z[x]/(x² + x + 1) = Z[ω] with cone N[1, −ω²] (semiring spanned by two units)
connection: The N-span of 1 and −ω² (a 60° wedge spanned by two units) is closed under addition; closure under multiplication needs checking ((−ω²)² = ω⁴ = ω, outside the wedge?). Cone design determines whether an Eisenstein twin exists.
why: If no multiplicatively closed discrete cone exists in Z[ω] with full rank, then the Eisenstein world has no faithful ES twin — a structural fact.
first_step: Enumerate small candidate cones generated by units/small elements and test multiplicative closure computationally.

title: Integer statement from the Gaussian twin: ES with denominators of the form a² + b² and a 'sector' constraint
connection: A Gaussian-cone solution for rational p projects (via norms) to an integer equation with denominators that are sums of two squares. The norm-constrained integer world fails at 40 primes below 2·10^4, so any projection must lose this constraint somewhere.
why: Quantifies what the Gaussian world can and cannot give back to Z: norms alone are too restrictive.
first_step: For a few p in the norm-failure list (41, 137), check whether Gaussian-cone solutions exist (if yes, the projection is not via norms).

title: ES for Gaussian n = π with π ≡ 1 mod 4 in Z[i] but denominators in Z (rational): mixed world
connection: Ask for 4/π = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x, y, z ∈ Z[i] but two of them rational integers. Mixing rational and Gaussian denominators interpolates between ES and the Gaussian twin.
why: Mixed worlds test whether a single 'extra' algebraic denominator suffices to dissolve difficulty (one complex degree of freedom).
first_step: Brute-force for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 2000 with two rational denominators.

title: One algebraic denominator: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/α with α ∈ O_K totally positive, x, y ∈ ℕ
connection: Allowing exactly one denominator from a real quadratic O_K (totally positive) while the others are integers. Then 1/α must be rational, so α is rational unless 1/x + 1/y is irrational — impossible. So this world collapses to ES (or to two algebraic denominators).
why: Shows that algebraic denominators come in conjugate pairs at minimum; the minimal interesting mixed world has 2 algebraic + 1 rational denominator (the trace-norm binary-form item).
first_step: Record; pursue the 2+1 world (batch B 'quadratic orbit ES').

title: ES with denominators in a fixed coset of squares: 4/n = Σ 1/(c·s_i²)
connection: Denominators c·s² (c fixed squarefree): 4/(cn)… reduces to 4c'/n = Σ 1/s_i², the square-reciprocal world (batch C). A coset choice c = p makes it p-tied.
why: Square-reciprocal worlds are very sparse; their solvability for specific c might be governed by genus theory, giving a quadratic-forms handle.
first_step: For c ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 6} compute which n admit 4/n = Σ 1/(c s_i²) up to 10^5.

title: ES over the semiring of Pythagorean triples / norm-one elements: Z[i] units of infinite order? none — use Q(i)^×/torsion
connection: Category check: Z[i] has finite units, so a 'norm-one cone' is finite; using Q(i) norm-one elements gives non-integral denominators. Not a meaningful world; recorded as closed.
why: Avoids a dead end.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Gaussian-cone ES for rational p counted by Hecke characters
connection: Solutions in Z[i] with sector constraints correspond to Gaussian integers in angular sectors; counts of Gaussian primes/integers in sectors are given by Hecke Grössencharacters (Kubilius). A sector-count formula for Gaussian-cone ES would use equidistribution of angles.
why: Angular equidistribution is proved (Hecke); if ES's Gaussian twin reduces to 'some solution in a sector', equidistribution of all solutions' angles would prove it for large norm.
first_step: Compute angles of all Z[i] solutions of 4/p (no cone) for p ≤ 1000 and check whether some lies in the cone; test equidistribution.

title: Z[i] without cone: solutions are plentiful; the cone is a 1/4-probability event per solution
connection: If unconstrained Gaussian solutions are many (polylog or more) and angles are equidistributed, the chance that all three denominators land in the cone is ≈ (1/4)³ per solution — so the Gaussian twin is a lottery with known ticket probability.
why: A clean model where the 'lottery' probability is geometric (angles), enabling exact heuristics to compare with the integer lottery.
first_step: Measure the fraction of unconstrained Gaussian solutions with all denominators in the cone for p ≤ 1000.

title: Gaussian numerator ladder: (1+i)^k/π for k = 1..4 interpolates between 2/n (trivial) and 4/n
connection: In Z[i], 4 = −(1+i)⁴, so the Gaussian-cone ES has numerator (1+i)⁴ up to a unit. The intermediate numerators (1+i)² = 2i and (1+i)³ give worlds 'between 2 and 4' that have no integer counterpart.
why: Locating the first k at which the Gaussian-cone problem becomes hard would show whether difficulty is tied to the full dyadic exponent (v_{(1+i)}(4) = 4) or appears earlier — a dyadic resolution invisible over Z.
first_step: Search for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 2000 whether (1+i)^k/π (k = 1, 2, 3) is a sum of three cone unit fractions; record failures per k.

title: Dyadic splitting type across imaginary quadratic twins: 2 ramified (Z[i]), inert (Z[ω]), split (Z[(1+√−7)/2])
connection: The numerator 4 factors differently: (1+i)⁴, 2² (inert), (αᾱ)² (split). If ES-type difficulty in cone worlds depends on how 2 splits, the dyadic structure of ES (I3 coordinate 4Z ∪ (8Z − p), m = 8 coincidence) is the integer shadow of that dependence.
why: Gives a controlled experiment on the role of the prime 2 with three otherwise similar worlds.
first_step: Define comparable cones in the three rings (discrete, multiplicatively closed) and compare failure statistics for rational primes p ≤ 2000.

title: Cone worlds in Z[√2]: compare four cones (ℕ, N[√2], height-positive, totally positive)
connection: A family of four cones in one ring, only partially ordered by inclusion (e.g. √2 ∈ N[√2] is not totally positive), with expected behaviour hard, ?, hard?, easy. Measuring solution counts per cone for rational p gives a direct map of how cone size controls ES.
why: The cleanest single-ring experiment for the cone principle.
first_step: Implement one search with four filters; output solution counts per cone for p ≤ 1000.

title: ES for Hurwitz quaternions of prime norm p: does every p have a quaternion solution with commuting denominators?
connection: Commuting quaternion denominators lie in an imaginary quadratic subfield; so quaternion ES with commuting denominators = union over imaginary quadratic orders inside the quaternion order of cone-ES there.
why: Gives a union-of-imaginary-quadratic-twins world: ES over many Gaussian-like rings at once; existence in at least one might be easy.
first_step: For p ≤ 500, search for quaternion solutions with all denominators in a common Z[√−d] ⊂ Hurwitz order.

title: Category-error check: 'ES in the field of p-adic numbers with absolute value positivity'
connection: Q_p has no ordering, and |x|_p ≥ 1 is not closed under addition; so 'positive' p-adic ES with |·|_p-positivity is ill-defined beyond cones of units (collapse) — record as closed.
why: Avoids repeated reconsideration.
first_step: None (closed).

title: ES with denominators from a lacunary set (powers times small factors): 4/p = Σ 1/(a_i 2^{k_i})
connection: Denominators of the form small·2^k: 4/p − Σ … requires p | some denominator, so at least one denominator is p·(small)·2^k; the problem becomes a 2-adic digit problem for (stuff)/p — likely solvable only for special p (p | 2^k − small).
why: A lacunary world tied to the multiplicative order of 2 mod p: ES-type solvability ⇔ conditions on ord_p(2), an Artin-type problem.
first_step: For p < 5000, test solvability with denominators a·2^k (a ≤ 15) times p^{0,1}; correlate with ord_p(2).

title: Feature: Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)'. ES LACKS: ES needs divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C of linear forms, which no cyclotomic structure forces. To supply it one could: use Lucas sequences U_n(P,Q) with discriminant D: primitive divisors r of U_n satisfy r ≡ (D/r) mod n, so negative D gives r ≡ −1 mod n for inert r — choose (P,Q) depending on p
why: Zsigmondy/BHV force divisors in classes ±1 mod n; a −1 mod 4C class appears naturally for inert primes.
first_step: Construct for given p a Lucas sequence whose n-th term equals (or divides) 4Cp+1 or a related ES integer; check whether its primitive divisors can be forced inert.

title: Transfer: Smith's method: ES 'spin' distribution
connection: Koymans–Milovic and Smith control 2-power class group ranks via bilinear 'spin' sums. ES's Type I success for fixed (a,d) is a Jacobi-symbol-type condition on p; the joint distribution over many (a,d) might be a spin system.
why: Smith's method proves 100% results when pointwise criteria lack governing fields — exactly ES's apparent situation.
first_step: Check whether the indicator of 'p solved by (a,d)' can be written via Jacobi symbols (p/q) for q | 4a²d+1 and how they interact for different (a,d).

title: Transfer: Gaussian-integer lifting of ES
connection: Over ℤ[i], p = ππ̄ splits. Write 4/p = 4/(ππ̄) and look for Gaussian-integer representations that descend to rational ones (norms/traces).
why: Splitting of p ≡ 1 mod 4 is the extra structure available exactly at ES's hard primes.
first_step: Search for identities 4/(ππ̄) = Σ 1/ξ_i with ξ_i ∈ ℤ[i] such that conjugate pairs combine into rational unit fractions.

title: Minimal pair: Artin conjecture (conditional) vs existence of a primitive root (proved)
connection: Artin conjecture (conditional) vs existence of a primitive root (proved): they differ essentially in one feature — fixed base a vs free choice of base. ES's position: ES has free choice of certificate parameters (like free base), which suggests existence should be easier than an Artin-type fixed-witness statement.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: Quantify how much freedom ES has: number of 'independent' parameters vs constraint count.

title: Minimal pair: Ramanujan's form x²+y²+10z² (finite exceptions, GRH) vs x²+y²+z² (proved by genus)
connection: Ramanujan's form x²+y²+10z² (finite exceptions, GRH) vs x²+y²+z² (proved by genus): they differ essentially in one feature — class number of the genus > 1 (spinor genus not a single class). ES's position: ES has no class-number parametrisation at all; closer to the harder member.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: None.

title: Feature: p-adic / archimedean transition (local densities at ∞)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'p-adic / archimedean transition (local densities at ∞)'. ES positivity region is bounded (finitely many positive solutions). To supply it one could: view the positive solutions as integral points in a compact region of a non-compact surface; volume of region ~ log² p (matches count)
why: Counting in bounded regions with volume → ∞ slowly is the generic 'small count' regime; proofs require effective equidistribution at log scale.
first_step: Compute the volume of the positivity region in Haar/log measure and compare with R(p) on average.

title: Arithmetic statistics of 'ES-failing residue systems' (Cohen–Lenstra style)
connection: Model the subgroups H_C ∌ −1 confining N_C's factors as random subgroups; Cohen–Lenstra-type weights might give the right probabilities for simultaneous confinement.
why: Arithmetic statistics heuristics with correct weights often predict exceptional sets accurately (e.g. Stevenhagen's negative Pell).
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of the subgroup generated by N_C's prime factors in (ℤ/4C)^× for fixed small C over many p.

title: a_p(32a1) mod 8 is just (2/p)
connection: The strong correlation of U(p) with a_p(y²=x³−x) mod 8 (ρ=+0.55) is identical to that with (2/p) (ρ=−0.55): for this CM curve a_p mod 8 encodes p mod 8.
why: Records a spurious-looking modular-form 'match' and its trivial explanation (guard against false fingerprints).
first_step: None needed; use as a sanity check whenever a CM form correlates.

title: h(−3p) correlates positively with U(p) (ρ=+0.46)
connection: U(p) residual vs h(−3p) (imaginary quadratic field Q(√−3p)) ρ = +0.46; vs h(−4p) only +0.08 (raw) / +0.14 (normalised).
why: χ_{−3p}(q) = (−3/q)(p/q): another twist; ES identities with denominator 3 (p ≡ 2 mod 3 classes) suggest the −3 twist is natural.
first_step: Fit log U on all of log L(1,χ_{dp}) for d ∈ {1,−1,−3,−4,−8,5,−20,…} jointly and identify the minimal set.

title: Higher-power residue characters of 2,3,5,7 have no detectable effect on ES counts
connection: Within strata of fixed quadratic profile ((2/p),(3/p),(5/p),(7/p)), whether a ∈ {2,3,5,7} is a cubic/quartic/octic residue mod p shifts mean residual log U(p), k₁, k₂, R(p) by |Δ| ≤ 0.03 (largest −0.029; the attached Mann–Whitney p-values are unstratified tests, smallest 0.015 among 48 tests — consistent with null after multiple testing).
why: Data counterpart of the genus/higher-character split (FRONTIER §2.1): order ≥ 3 characters at small primes don't bias counts; all systematic arithmetic dependence is quadratic (plus p−1 structure).
first_step: Repeat with characters of order 3,4 of larger moduli (q ≤ 50) and with the full X(n) decomposition on (★).

title: 2-adic depth matters: p ≡ 1 (16) has 9% fewer ES solutions than p ≡ 9 (16)
connection: Among p ≡ 1 (8), residual log U(p) is lower by 0.094 when p ≡ 1 (16) (k₁ −0.098, k₂ −0.080, R −0.051); next level 32 vs 16 only −0.013; 9 vs 3: −0.030; 25 vs 5: −0.021.
why: Not explained by quadratic characters ((2/p) = 1 in both classes) nor by the quartic character of 2 (null): it is the multiplicative depth of p−1 at 2 — local densities of the ES surface at 2 depend on p mod 16.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic local density of {4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z} as a function of p mod 2^k and compare to the observed 9% gap.

title: Quartic residuosity of 2 (p = x² + 64y²) is irrelevant for ES counts
connection: Among p ≡ 1 (8), '2 is a 4th power mod p' shifts residual log U by +0.008 (MW p = 0.10).
why: Rules out a tempting Gauss-type link (p = x²+64y²) to hardness; the Neumann–Setzer form p = u²+64 is a different condition (see next item).
first_step: None needed; record as negative fingerprint.

title: Real class number h(p) is uncorrelated with U(p) (−0.04)
connection: Since h(p) = 1 for most p ≡ 1 (4) at this size, only the regulator carries the L-value; h(p) alone is uninformative.
why: Negative fingerprint: avoids chasing 'class group of Q(√p)' explanations.
first_step: None.

title: r₃(p) = 12 h(−4p) for p ≡ 1 (4): ES counts vs sums of three squares
connection: By Gauss, r₃(p) = 12h(−4p) at p ≡ 1 (mod 4); so U's weak correlation with h(−4p) (+0.08 raw, +0.14 normalised) is also its correlation with r₃(p).
why: THREE_SQUARES.md explored ES ↔ ternary forms; data say the three-squares count is only a weak predictor — the right ternary form, if any, is not x²+y²+z².
first_step: Correlate U(p) with representation numbers of other ternary forms of small discriminant (genus theory via Hurwitz numbers H(4p), H(8p), H(3p)).

title: Hurwitz class numbers H(4p), H(8p), H(3p) jointly vs ES counts
connection: Hurwitz numbers are coefficients of weight-3/2 Eisenstein series; a linear combination of H(dp)/√p could match the χ-twist dependence found for k₁/k₂.
why: Would give a modular-form 'shadow' of the ES main term, testable to high precision.
first_step: Fit log k₂ on log H(4p)/√p, log H(8p)/√p, log H(3p)/√p; inspect coefficients for rational structure.

title: ord_p(2)/(p−1) correlates +0.45 with U(p)
connection: Higher multiplicative order of 2 mod p ⇒ more solutions; partly via (2/p) (2 is a QNR ⇒ index odd…), partly via p−1 smoothness.
why: Artin-type data (order of 2) is a cheap proxy that might enter ES via 2-power denominators (TWO_POWER_LADDER.md).
first_step: Partial correlation controlling for (2/p) and τ(p−1); compare with ord_p(3), ord_p(5).

title: ES hardness vs Wieferich-type / Fermat-quotient data
connection: Compute-and-check: correlation of U(p) with q_p(2) = (2^{p−1} − 1)/p mod p (Fermat quotient) — a p-adic invariant of 2.
why: Would test whether p-adic (mod p²) information about small primes affects ES; expected null, but cheap and a clean negative.
first_step: Compute q_p(2) mod p for p ≤ 2·10⁵, normalise to [0,1), Spearman with residual U.

title: Proth-type primes k·2^n + 1 with small k as an ES-hardness test bed
connection: Primes k·2^n+1 (k ≤ 15) have deep 2-adic structure and controllable p−1; scanning U(p)/log² over them separates 2-adic depth from other effects.
why: Large known families (Proth primes) give hard-ish test primes at sizes 10⁶–10¹² where generic censuses are too expensive.
first_step: List Proth primes ≤ 10⁸ and compute R(p), U(p) via targeted solvers.

title: ES hardness index vs class number of Q(ζ_p)^+? (too expensive; proxy via h(p))
connection: Compute-and-check (proxy): cyclotomic class-number data are unavailable at scale; the quadratic subfield Q(√p) (h(p) null) is the only cheap proxy.
why: Records that the cyclotomic-unit / Vandiver-type world shows no signal at the quadratic level.
first_step: Skip unless a specific cyclotomic mechanism is proposed.

title: At odd n, every solution has at least two even denominators
connection: Exactly-0-even and exactly-1-even solutions never occur at primes (2-adic parity: three odd unit fractions sum to odd/odd; one even denominator gives odd numerator over even); shares: 2 even 52%, all even 48%.
why: Trivial 2-adic lemma but a useful normal form: write x = 2x₁ or the pair y, z even; reduces 2-adic case analysis in parametrisations.
first_step: None beyond writing down the lemma.

title: Composite failures for 'none of x, y, z divisible by 4': exactly multiples of 16
connection: Among n ≤ 3000 the n with no ES solution having 4 ∤ x, 4 ∤ y, 4 ∤ z are 16, 32, 48, …; the analogous condition for 8 fails exactly at multiples of 32, for 9 at multiples of 9, for 5 at multiples of 5.
why: Clean local lemmas (p-adic valuation of n forces valuations of denominators); sanity checks for the variant engine.
first_step: Prove: v₂(n) ≥ 4 ⇒ 4 | some denominator; v₃(n) ≥ 2 ⇒ 9 | some denominator.

title: Markov primes vs 12/p failures: {2, 5, 13, 29, 433} = Markov ∩ fail(12) ≤ 10⁵
connection: Markov primes ≤ 10⁵: 2,5,13,29,89,233,433,1597,2897,5741,7561,28657,33461,43261,96557; five lie in the 22-element 12/p failure set (and the same five in fail(24)); 433 is the notable one.
why: Probably small-number coincidence, but Markov numbers m have −1 and other small quantities as QRs mod m (m | a²+b² with structured a, b) — a quadratic-residue profile like ES-hard primes; MARKOFF_ES.md explores Markov ↔ ES.
first_step: Compute the least QNR / L(1,χ_m) quantile for Markov primes and test enrichment in all m/p failure sets with a permutation test.

title: Pell numerology: R-zeros 409 = 408 + 1 and 577 with 577² − 2·408² = 1
connection: The first two (★) failures are 408+1 and 577, the Pell pair (577, 408) for √2; 577 − 1 = 24².
why: Almost certainly coincidence; recorded because √2-convergents p/q give p ≡ ±1 structure and 2 is a QR mod both — test cheaply with the next Pell pairs (3363, 2378), (19601, 13860).
first_step: Check R(p) at primes near Pell numbers (2379, 3361? 3363 is composite; 13861, 19601 composite) — expect nothing.

title: Type number of quaternion orders vs ES counts
connection: The type number of B_{p,∞} has class-number correction terms (h(−4p), h(−8p), h(−3p)) whose weighting resembles our twist fits; QUATERNION_ES.md relates ES to quaternion orders.
why: If ES counts correlate with the *correction terms* (after removing (p−1)/12 growth), the quaternion picture has a quantitative fingerprint.
first_step: Compute type numbers via Pizer/Eichler formulas for p ≤ 10⁵ and correlate their corrections with residual U, k₂.

title: Rank of y² = x³ − p²x / congruent-number curve at p vs ES count
connection: Congruent number curve E_p: y² = x³ − p²x; Tunnell's criterion decides positive rank / congruence (sufficiency conditional on BSD; it does not give the rank); primes p ≡ 5, 7 (8) are congruent (Heegner/Monsky). Compare U(p) by Tunnell class.
why: Tunnell's criterion counts ternary-form representations (x²+2y²+8z² = p) — a theta-series fingerprint; ES may correlate with these ternary counts.
first_step: Compute Tunnell's counts A(p), B(p) for p ≤ 10⁵ and Spearman with residual U(p).

title: ES counts on the 'norm form' side: n = a² + b² with a/b fixed angle
connection: For n ≡ 1 (4) prime the Gaussian angle was null; for composite n test whether representations as norms from Z[ω], Z[√−2] (x²+3y², x²+2y²) predict counts.
why: Norm-form representability is the genus/class-field data; for primes it reduces to Legendre symbols (already captured), for composites it adds multiplicities.
first_step: Correlate U(n) with r_{x²+y²}(n), r_{x²+2y²}(n), r_{x²+3y²}(n) at composites ≤ 30 000.

title: Tunnell's ternary counts: individually weakly correlated with residual U (ρ ≈ 0.18), Tunnell difference A − 2B null (0.02)
connection: For p ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8), 100 < p ≤ 2·10⁴ (1 115 primes): #{x²+2y²+8z² = p} and #{x²+2y²+32z² = p} each correlate +0.19/+0.18 with residual log U(p); A − 2B (congruent-number criterion) ≈ 0.
why: The weight-3/2 theta coefficients share the class-number/genus signal (both ∝ h(−8p)-type quantities) but the congruent-number combination carries nothing: no congruent-number ↔ ES link at the data level.
first_step: Correlate with h(−2p), h(−8p) to confirm the shared signal is just the class number.

title: Saturation and boundary components
connection: Study the ideal of 4xyz−p(xy+xz+yz) after excluding zero coordinates and compare its components under congruence restrictions.
why: Removing degenerate solutions is essential before algebraic parametrizations are interpreted arithmetically.
first_step: Compute the saturation by xyz for a small symbolic specialization and inspect the nonzero locus.

title: Norm equations
connection: Rewrite selected quadratic discriminant conditions as norms in quadratic orders and track the congruences needed for ES.
why: Multiplicativity of norms may combine certificates in ways raw divisor enumeration misses.
first_step: For one Pell-type slice, translate the equation into a norm and record its positivity restrictions.

title: Class-group bookkeeping
connection: When a divisor condition factors in a quadratic order, distinguish principal from nonprincipal ideal factors.
why: This identifies an arithmetic constraint that could guide which auxiliary field is useful.
first_step: For a small negative discriminant arising from a slice, compare ideal factorizations with actual integral certificates.

title: Reciprocity as a design constraint
connection: Rather than discard square-like obstructions, use quadratic reciprocity to choose parameters with deliberately opposite symbols.
why: Symbols can guide which certificate family is worth trying at each prime.
first_step: For a small family, derive the Legendre-symbol necessary conditions and search complementary parameter choices.

title: Nonunit residue handling
connection: Separate auxiliary prime factors sharing the modulus from unit factors before applying group-based divisor heuristics.
why: Ignoring nonunits would make the group model false; stratifying valuations repairs it.
first_step: Implement a residue-state enumeration that tracks gcd with the modulus and compare it with unit-only counts.

title: Cyclotomic factor opportunities
connection: Choose auxiliary parameters making a p-tied expression resemble a cyclotomic value with structured factors.
why: Algebraic factorization can manufacture divisors, although the required residue must still be checked.
first_step: Search low-degree substitutions yielding a difference of squares or a cyclotomic factorization in the residual equation.

title: Reciprocity-induced correlation
connection: Track how reciprocity couples residue information about p and its auxiliary factors.
why: Treating those symbols as independent would obscure exact constraints that might guide construction.
first_step: Tabulate both directions of Legendre symbols for successful certificates and derive the forced sign relation.

title: Partition reciprocity as a sanity tool
connection: Compare positive and nonnegative lattice-point counts in polyhedral relaxations of denominator constraints.
why: Boundary corrections may identify which apparent certificates are merely zero or infinite-denominator artifacts.
first_step: Construct a simple linearized divisor-allocation polytope and compare interior with closed lattice-point counts.

title: Contingency-table factor allocations
connection: Arrange prime valuations in a table indexed by factors and denominator components, with row totals fixed.
why: This creates a familiar integer-fiber problem for the multiplicative part of certificate construction.
first_step: Enumerate valuation tables for an auxiliary integer with three prime factors and compare their induced congruence outcomes.

title: Petri nets for denominator resources
connection: Model valuation transfers under exact identity moves as token transitions between denominator components.
why: Conservation laws in the net may reveal which transformations can or cannot connect two families.
first_step: Derive a token transition from one exact move and compute its linear invariants.

title: Arithmetic tori from norm-one units
connection: Use norm-one units to move along a norm-equation slice while preserving its right-hand side.
why: The remaining question becomes whether the orbit reaches the positivity and congruence region needed for ES.
first_step: For a small real quadratic norm equation, compute unit-orbit residues modulo the required modulus.

title: p-adic dynamics of parameter maps
connection: Iterate an exact rational parameter transformation over residue rings and inspect attracting or periodic classes.
why: Stable modular behavior could support iterative congruence repair before real positivity is addressed.
first_step: For a verified map, enumerate its defined orbits modulo 3² and 3³ and compare lifting patterns.

title: Harmonic analysis beyond the unit group
connection: Use the full multiplicative residue monoid when auxiliary factors are not units, rather than forcing a group model.
why: A monoid representation can retain valuation strata that ordinary character expansions omit.
first_step: Construct multiplication operators on residues modulo 12 and decompose their invariant subspaces.

title: FFT convolution on cyclic residue coordinates
connection: Use discrete-log coordinates in a cyclic unit group to turn divisor-selection convolution into cyclic convolution.
why: Fast convolution can count residue witnesses exactly with suitable integer reconstruction.
first_step: For a small prime modulus, compare direct dynamic programming with an exact convolution implementation.

title: Galois actions on factor-allocation types
connection: Study how algebraic conjugation permutes possible factors in a norm-based parametrization.
why: Invariant allocations may descend to rational or integer expressions that are not obvious in split coordinates.
first_step: For one quadratic-field slice, list conjugate factor assignments and compute their invariant products and traces.

title: Genus-two slices as stress tests
connection: Impose a simple additional relation and check whether a higher-genus curve appears with a few explicit certificate points.
why: Such slices can reveal which constraints make a family too rigid while still providing concrete finite examples.
first_step: Try a cubic relation between two denominators, compute the curve genus, and inspect the known points without assuming completeness.

title: Eisenstein and cusp contribution separation
connection: For a valid modular count, separate an explicit main contribution from the cusp contribution before assessing positivity.
why: The decomposition could reveal the exact estimate needed for one slice, without assuming it is available.
first_step: Locate the modular space for a concrete theta series and determine whether its Eisenstein projection can be computed at low level.

title: Complex multiplication specializations
connection: Look for special quadratic parameters where norm or theta expressions simplify through extra algebraic symmetry.
why: Special values might yield isolated constructive families rather than uniform coverage.
first_step: Choose a small discriminant, compute the associated norm expressions, and test whether the ES congruences simplify.

title: Spinor-genus diagnostics on quadratic slices
connection: Check whether local representation conditions for a selected quadratic form split into globally different arithmetic classes.
why: The goal is to understand that slice's representation pattern, not to infer an obstruction for ES as a whole.
first_step: Compute small representation data for a concrete ternary form and check literature on its genus and spinor genus.

title: Local-to-global comparison in a fixed slice
connection: Compare exact integer representations with solvability modulo increasing moduli for one explicitly derived quadratic subproblem.
why: A discrepancy identifies what extra arithmetic data the slice requires while leaving other families untouched.
first_step: For a small form and target range, enumerate representations and modular solutions with a common documented bound.

title: p-adic variation of modular counts
connection: If a valid modular family of representation counts exists, compare its coefficients as an auxiliary weight or level varies p-adically.
why: Variation may reveal congruence relations useful for selecting a family, not universal nonvanishing by itself.
first_step: Choose one verified modular family and check whether its coefficient congruences fit a known p-adic interpolation framework.

title: Local zeta functions of certificate congruences
connection: Count solutions of a fixed auxiliary polynomial system modulo powers of a prime and package the counts in a generating function.
why: The local zeta data may reveal stable lifting patterns and singular branches.
first_step: For a small odd prime q, count solutions modulo q and q² in a bounded-dimensional model and separate singular from nonsingular classes.

title: p-adic integrals for valuation distributions
connection: Express a local valuation histogram as an integral over residue classes and compare it with direct enumeration.
why: This provides a compact language for how divisibility conditions interact across powers of one prime.
first_step: For one auxiliary polynomial, compute the proportions with valuation 0,1,2 modulo a sufficiently high prime power.

title: Newton polygons for valuation branches
connection: Apply Newton-polygon analysis to a one-variable polynomial arising after fixing auxiliary parameters.
why: The slopes can constrain valuations of possible roots and guide which congruence lifts deserve attention.
first_step: For a quadratic or cubic residual polynomial, draw its Newton polygon at a small prime and compare predicted root valuations with exact examples.

title: Aharonov–Bohm phase / holonomy around the odd-square obstruction
connection: T1 says certificate lines are empty at odd squares for a reciprocity reason. A 'holonomy' interpretation: going around the square locus in the (p, C) parameter plane picks up a sign (Jacobi symbol). Mechanisms with nontrivial holonomy are forced to fail at squares — which is exactly what the barrier demands of any proof.
why: Reformulating T1 as a topological phase might guide the design of a mechanism that *provably* has the right failure mode at squares.
first_step: Write the Jacobi symbol (−C/p)-type sign that vanishes/flips at squares as a function on the parameter plane; check whether it is the Brauer class of Bright–Loughran evaluated at the fibre.

title: Scattering theory: 4/p as a resonance of the Eisenstein series at a cusp
connection: The Eisenstein series Fourier coefficients involve divisor sums σ_s(n); divisor-type counts restricted to residue classes appear in Eisenstein series for Γ₀(4C). The number of divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C is a coefficient of an Eisenstein series on Γ₁(4C).
why: Converts the tied-modulus divisor count into a modular-form coefficient; sign/positivity of such coefficients across the level is a studied question (for Eisenstein series, coefficients are explicit character sums).
first_step: Write d_{−1 mod 4C}(4Cp+1) as (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ̄(−1) Σ_{d|4Cp+1} χ(d) and see whether summing over C turns the inner twisted divisor sum into something with a known positive main term (repo's M_BM?).

title: Z₂ gauge theory on the prime-factor hypergraph of {4Cp+1}_C
connection: Each C gives a set of primes; a sign assignment (Legendre symbol (q/·)) on primes is a Z₂ gauge field; ES requires a 'Wilson loop' (product of symbols) to equal a target at some C. Gauge-invariant content = the frustration pattern.
why: Gauge-theoretic language can isolate what is invariant under rechoosing C; T1 (squares) is manifestly gauge-invariant.
first_step: Write the product of Legendre symbols Π (−p/q) over q | 4Cp+1 and relate to the divisor-class condition via reciprocity; check whether a known 'reciprocity sign' identity makes the product identically computable.

title: Fluctuation theorem / Jarzynski: average over C of exponential weights gives pointwise-in-p identities
connection: Jarzynski's equality turns an average of exp(−W) into a free-energy difference exactly, for every realization of the system. Analogue: an *exact* identity Σ_C w(C)·(#divisors of 4Cp+1 in class) = known function of p would be a 'fluctuation theorem' for ES.
why: Exact identities for weighted divisor sums over C at fixed p do exist (they are class-number-type formulas: Σ_C d_χ(4Cp+1) relates to L-values); positivity then becomes an L-value statement.
first_step: Search for exact formulas: Σ_{C ≤ X} Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} χ_{4C}(d) in terms of class numbers (Hurwitz–Kronecker type); check FRONTIER §2 M_BM derivation for what identity is used.

title: Conformal-field-theory c=1 / Gaussian free field model of Dedekind sums tied to 4/p
connection: Dedekind sums s(a,c) satisfy reciprocity and are governed by continued fractions; continued-fraction length λ(p) ≤ 3 (ES₅) might be expressible through Dedekind-sum identities (Rademacher's 3-term reciprocity).
why: Rademacher's three-term Dedekind reciprocity is exactly a 'three-term' relation — a formal resemblance to three unit fractions worth 30 minutes.
first_step: Write the ES₅ rational, compute its Dedekind sum, and test numerically whether ES solutions correspond to triples (a,b,c) in Rademacher's identity s(a,b)+s(b,c)+s(c,a) = ... with a 1/12-type constant involving 4/p.
refs: Rademacher, 'Generalization of the reciprocity formula for Dedekind sums' (1954)

title: Symbolic regression on f(p) to find a closed-form main term with explicit arithmetic corrections
connection: Fit f(p) ≈ A log²p + B log p · g(p) + ... where g ranges over arithmetic features (number of prime factors of p−1, p+1, class number h(−p), h(−4p), least QNR, Legendre symbols of small primes).
why: If a class-number or L-value feature explains a large part of the variance, it hints that f(p) is 'really' a class-number-type quantity (which would be an exact-formula route).
first_step: Build a feature table for primes ≤ 10⁶ (h(−4p), h(−p), ω(p±1), (2/p),(3/p),(5/p),(7/p), smallest prime factor of 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1 …); run PySR/LASSO on f(p)/log²p; report R².

title: Binary quadratic forms: Type I as representation of p² by a form of discriminant −16c²d
connection: f | p² + 4c²d means p² + 4c²d = f·g; representation theory of binary quadratic forms (Gauss composition) describes which f occur as 'first coefficients' of forms representing p² + 4c²d... Equivalently, (p, c·2√(−d)) is a vector in an imaginary quadratic order; the norm factorisation is governed by the class group of ℚ(√−d).
why: Class-group structure of ℤ[√−d] is *rigid* and the 'divisor in a residue class' condition on f may translate into a *genus* condition (which is a character condition, computable), leaving the class-group part.
first_step: Write the Type I condition in the order O_d = ℤ[2c√−d]: f is the norm of an ideal dividing (p + 2c√−d)? Check: N(p + 2c√−d) = p² + 4c²d. So f | N(α) for α = p + 2c√−d; ideal divisors of (α) have norms f; the residue condition f ≡ −p mod 4cd is a condition on the ideal class modulo 4cd (ray class group). Verify this translation numerically.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Primes p for which 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1, … are all 'sums of two squares type': structure of the joint exceptional set
connection: Following the C=1 criterion: the failure set for C ≤ K is {p : for every C ≤ K, 4Cp + 1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C}. For C with 4C having few residue classes ≡ −1 the condition is 'all prime factors in a subgroup' — a multiplicative-structure condition (like 'n is a norm from ℚ(i)').
why: Norm-type sets have Dirichlet-series descriptions (Landau), so the joint failure set for C ≤ K has a computable density ~ Π_C (1 − something)^(…) and a *structure* (a norm from a compositum?). If the joint failure set for all C were provably empty by a norm argument… that's ES. But at least the per-C structure is exact.
first_step: For C = 1,2,3: characterise 'no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C' exactly in terms of prime factorisation (subgroup H_C ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× not containing −1 and all factors in H_C? Not quite — subset products must avoid −1, which for a subgroup H ∌ −1 means all factors in H; else more complex). Tabulate for C ≤ 10.

title: Kummer/Galois reformulation: ES ⟸ ∃C: some prime factor q of 4Cp+1 has Frobenius outside a fixed subgroup of Gal(ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ)
connection: If the subgroup criterion holds, then C wins whenever some prime q | 4Cp+1 has q mod 4C ∉ H for every −1-free subgroup H... Simplest: q ≡ −1 mod 4C directly (then q itself is the divisor). So a sufficient condition: 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C. Over C, this is 'the polynomial values 4Cp+1 (C varying, p fixed) have a prime factor in the class −1' — a statement about prime divisors of a linear polynomial in C at a fixed 'twist' p.
why: Prime divisors of values of linear forms in residue classes is a well-studied topic (e.g. Bang–Zsigmondy for a^n − 1, and 'prime factors of n! ± 1' type results); the fixed-p twist is unusual but concrete.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁶ the smallest C such that 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C (the 'prime-divisor' certificate); compare to C_min; search 'prime divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C'.

title: Reciprocity proof of T1 as a *template*: what is the exact Jacobi-symbol identity, and does its negation at non-squares produce a divisor?
connection: T1's proof: if m² = (ab − 1)/(4C) with a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C then ... a Jacobi symbol contradiction. At a non-square p, the same Jacobi symbol computation gives no contradiction but gives *information* — e.g., a constraint on (−C/p) or (p/a) that must hold for any certificate; this constraint is a 'necessary condition' on winning C, and might be the thing to make sufficient.
why: Necessary conditions on winning C from reciprocity (e.g. 'C must satisfy (−C/p) = +1'?) halve the search space; verify whether such a condition is known and whether data confirms it.
first_step: Derive: from 4Cp + 1 = ab, a ≡ −1 mod 4C: compute (a/p)·(b/p) = (ab/p) = (1/p) = 1, and (p/a) via reciprocity... obtain a condition on C mod p or (C/p). Test numerically which Jacobi symbols are forced for winning (C, a).

title: Theta correspondence / Siegel–Weil: representation numbers of p² by ternary forms as a positivity source
connection: Siegel–Weil gives representation numbers of quadratic forms as Eisenstein series values (positive main terms); ternary forms (3 variables) have local–global failures only at finitely many spinor exceptions. Type I: f·g = p² + 4c²d is a quaternary 'norm form' condition. Is there a ternary form Q with Q(c, …) = p² representation ⟺ a Type I certificate?
why: Representation by ternary forms with 'all large n represented' (Duke–Schulze-Pillot) is a proven pointwise theorem with log-size counts — close to ES's shape! It needs the form to be fixed; ES's 'form' varies with (c,d). Still, a fixed-form subfamily (e.g. d = 1 only) might inherit the theorem.
first_step: Fix d = 1: Type I with d = 1: f | p² + 4c² with f ≡ −p mod 4c. The equation p² + 4c² = fg with congruence — compare with representations of p² by the form x² + 4y² restricted by congruences; check whether Duke–Schulze-Pillot's theorem on 'all large n represented by a ternary form with congruence conditions' applies to some auxiliary ternary form.

title: Kronecker's limit formula / class number h(−4d) as the 'main term' for Type I at fixed d
connection: Σ_c #{f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (4cd)} over c ≤ X is a sum over representations by forms of discriminant −16d... whose total is controlled by class numbers; Kronecker–Hurwitz-type formulas give Σ_c r_Q(p² + 4c²d) in terms of h(−d·) and L(1, χ).
why: Exact class-number formulas are 'rigid' inputs; if the Type I count at fixed d has a class-number main term with an explicit error, choosing d with large h(−4d)/√d (many classes, small discriminant) maximises the main term.
first_step: For d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 7} compute the Type I count over c ≤ X numerically for p ≈ 10⁶ and compare with h(−4d)·log X·const; estimate the constant.

title: Mock modular forms / Zagier's weight-3/2 Eisenstein series for class-number generating functions evaluated at the ES data
connection: The generating function Σ H(n)q^n is a mock modular form (Zagier). The ES Type I count relates to H(p² + 4c²d) (previous item). Mock modularity gives asymptotics with *explicit* error terms for sums of H over quadratic sequences (via holomorphic projection / shadow).
why: Explicit error terms for 'class numbers along quadratic sequences p² + 4c²d in c' might, for a single p, give a positive main term exceeding the error — a pointwise statement! The size: main term ≍ X·√(p)... vs ES's count log²p — the class-number sum counts ALL divisors, not the residue-class-constrained ones; the constraint costs 1/φ(4cd), summing to ≈ log X. So the error term must be < log X — hopeless unless the error is tiny. Record the calculation.
first_step: Compute Σ_{c ≤ X} H(p² + 4c²) for p = 10⁶+3 and compare with main term; then the constrained count; tabulate the ratio.

title: Per-C exact sign structure: #{d | N, d ≡ −1 (m)} as a combination of multiplicative functions — the explicit product formula
connection: For m = 4C, #{d | N : d ≡ r (m)} = (1/φ(m)) Σ_χ χ̄(r) Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e). For N = 4Cp + 1 ≡ 1 mod m the trivial character contributes τ(N)/φ(m); each nontrivial χ contributes χ̄(−1)·Π(...). ES(p) fails at C iff these cancel exactly to 0. 'Exact cancellation of a sum of φ(m) products' is a strong algebraic condition.
why: The exact-cancellation view suggests an algebraic-number-theoretic approach: the sum is an algebraic integer in ℚ(ζ_{φ(m)})… no, it's rational; but the Π over characters is a norm-like expression. Cancellation to 0 might be ruled out by a *valuation* argument (2-adic valuation of τ(N)/φ(m) vs the rest) for suitable C — a rigidity mechanism!
first_step: Compute the 2-adic valuation of the trivial-character term τ(N)/φ(4C) and of the sum of nontrivial terms for failing (p, C); check whether failures require specific 2-adic coincidences; if a C with v₂-mismatch always exists, that's a proof direction.

title: Use the finite class group of ℚ(√−d) at Type I: choose d so that the class group is trivial (d ∈ {1,2,3,7,11,19,43,67,163}) and the divisor condition becomes a *splitting* condition
connection: For class number 1 fields, ideals = elements; f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) ⟺ p + 2c√−d = α·β in O_d with N(α) = f and a congruence on N(α). For h = 1, α is an actual element, so f = N(α) = s² + d t² (or the appropriate norm form) with a congruence on s² + dt² mod 4cd AND α | p + 2c√−d. This makes Type I at Heegner d's completely explicit in terms of representations of p + 2c√−d's divisors.
why: The nine Heegner discriminants give nine fully explicit sub-problems; Type I failures at all nine simultaneously would be a strong constraint on p; maybe the nine cases 'cover' primes by a non-polynomial reason (e.g., p's splitting pattern in the 9 fields = 9 Legendre symbols ⟹ 2⁹ profiles).
first_step: For each Heegner d and p ≤ 10⁶, compute whether a Type I solution with that d exists (c ≤ 10³); tabulate the 9-bit failure vector; check if any profile has all 9 failing.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Reciprocity-law zoo: Eisenstein reciprocity, Rédei symbols, Hilbert symbols — which one is T1 'really', and do its cousins give conditions at non-squares?
connection: T1 is proved by quadratic reciprocity; but the structure 'square ⟹ all certificates vanish' might be a special case of a reciprocity for a 4-term symbol (Rédei) or a Hilbert-symbol product formula (Π_v (a,b)_v = 1). The product formula is an *exact* global identity — if the ES certificate count mod 2 equals a Hilbert symbol product at some place, that's a parity theorem.
why: Parity theorems from the product formula are the standard rigid mechanism in 2-descent; ES's count mod 2 is unexplored (item on involutions).
first_step: Compute f_II(p) mod 2 and f_I(p) mod 2 for p ≤ 10⁶; test against Hilbert symbols (−1, p)_2, (2, p)_2, (p, −C)_q for small C, q; look for an exact parity formula.

title: Analogy with 'every integer is a sum of 3 triangular numbers' (Gauss) — a ternary representation theorem proved via class numbers; ES as a 'ternary' problem whose class-number formula is missing
connection: Gauss's Eureka theorem = r₃(8n+3) > 0 via h(−(8n+3)) > 0 — positivity of a class number! ES's Type I count at fixed d is governed by divisors of p² + 4c²d, i.e. by representations in ℚ(√−d); the analogue of 'h > 0' is the existence of an ideal of norm f in the right ray class — i.e., SURJECTIVITY of the Artin map onto a ray class group, which is Chebotarev-existence again.
why: Clarifies that ES's 'positivity' is of Artin-map-surjectivity type (every ray class contains an ideal dividing a specific (p + 2c√−d)) — a statement about ONE element's factorisation, hence B2; but it suggests looking at the *family over c* as a family of principal ideals (p + 2c√−d) whose ideal factors sweep the ray class group as c varies: do they equidistribute in the ray class group mod 4cd? (The modulus grows with c — a 'tied' equidistribution.)
first_step: For d = 1, p fixed, c ≤ X: compute the ray classes (mod 4c) of the ideal factors of (p + 2ci) in ℤ[i]; test equidistribution across c; identify the class containing the certificate.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Exceptional primes 409, 577, 5569, 9601: search for a second forced symbol via the 2-adic structure of a
connection: For C even (8 | 4C) we need a ≡ −1 mod 8; for C odd a ≡ 3 mod 4 only. The QNR condition (a/p) = −1 plus a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) plus a | 4Cp + 1. For p ≡ 1 mod 8 (577, 5569, 9601): (2/p) = 1 so the 2-part of a is irrelevant to (a/p)… The obstruction (if any) must come from the interplay of a mod 4C and a mod p via a | 4Cp+1: a ≡ −1 mod 4C and 4Cp ≡ −1 mod a. Consider the Jacobi symbol (a / (4Cp+1)/a) = (a/b): since a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4 … (a/b)(b/a) = −1 (both ≡ 3 mod 4); and (b/a) = (4Cp+1)/a … b ≡ (4Cp+1)/a; 4Cp+1 ≡ 1 mod a? No: a | 4Cp+1 so 4Cp+1 ≡ 0 mod a; b = (4Cp+1)/a, (b/a) = ? not determined. Hmm. Try instead a mod p: a·b ≡ 1 mod p, a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C: a + b ≡ −2 mod 4C and ab = 4Cp + 1: so (a + b + 2) ≡ 0 mod 4C and (a+1)(b+1) = ab + a + b + 1 = 4Cp + a + b + 2 ≡ 0 mod 4C — consistent. The pair (a, b) are roots of t² − s t + (4Cp+1) with s = a + b ≡ −2 mod 4C: discriminant s² − 4(4Cp+1) = (a − b)² must be a square. So C-form certificate ⟺ ∃ s ≡ −2 (mod 4C): s² − 16Cp − 4 is a perfect square ⟺ (s/2)² − 4Cp − 1 = (r)² with s/2 ≡ −1 mod 2C: ⟺ 4Cp + 1 = σ² − r² with σ ≡ −1 (mod 2C). So: C-form ⟺ 4Cp + 1 is a difference of two squares σ² − r² with σ ≡ −1 mod 2C (automatically σ ± r ≡ −1 mod 4C? need check). This 'difference of squares with a congruence' form is a new angle on the exceptions.
why: The 'σ² − r² with σ ≡ −1 mod 2C' form is a quadratic condition in two variables (σ, r) — suitable for genus/local analysis at the exceptional primes: for which p is σ² − r² = 4Cp + 1, σ ≡ −1 (2C) locally solvable for all C but globally never? Local solvability is presumably automatic; the exceptions would then be 'non-BM integral Hasse failures' of a FAMILY of conics — which is exactly the kind of phenomenon the Bright–Loughran framework studies.
first_step: Verify the equivalence (σ² − r² = 4Cp+1, σ ≡ −1 mod 2C ⟺ C-form certificate) numerically; then for p = 409, run the local analysis: for each C, is there a local obstruction (mod powers of 2, mod primes dividing C) to σ² − r² = 4·409·C + 1 with σ ≡ −1 mod 2C? If always locally solvable, the exceptions are integral Hasse failures — report.

title: Are the C-form exceptions 409, 577, 5569, 9601 exactly the primes p ≡ 1 mod 24 for which some hidden invariant (e.g. h(−4p) ≡ 0 mod 8, or p = x² + 64y²-type quartic condition) holds?
connection: 577 = 1² + 24², 409 = 3² + 20², 5569 = ? , 9601 = ?: compute p = x² + y² and look at 8 | y or 16 | y (which encode (2/p)_4 and higher 2-power symbols); also class numbers h(−p), h(−4p), h(−8p) and their 2-parts; and whether 2 is a quartic/octic residue mod p.
why: The exceptions are a tiny set; a matching invariant would turn 'finite accidents' into a 'quadratic/quartic obstruction' family (à la HKRS), which — since these primes DO have Type II solutions with c ≥ 2 — would show precisely what the c-parameter buys.
first_step: Compute for all primes ≡ 1 mod 24 below 20000 the invariants (x, y with p = x² + y², v₂(y), h(−4p) mod 16, quartic character of 2, p mod 48/96) and find any invariant that separates the four exceptions from the rest.

title: Could the C-form exceptional set be 'odd squares ∪ {p : (2/p)… something} ∪ finite' with the exceptions explained by a *quartic* reciprocity law?
connection: HKRS's Apollonian obstructions include quartic ones; the C-form's forced (a/p) = −1 is quadratic. A quartic analogue would be: when p ≡ 1 mod 8 and ... the quartic symbol (a/p)_4 is forced to a value that contradicts (a/p) = −1. For p ≡ 1 mod 8 (577, 5569, 9601 all ≡ 1 mod 8!; 409 ≡ 1 mod 8 too: 409 = 408 + 1 = 8·51 + 1 ✓). All four exceptions are ≡ 1 mod 8 — consistent with a quartic (mod 8-sensitive) obstruction acting on a subset of the p ≡ 1 mod 8 primes. Most primes ≡ 1 mod 8 do have certificates, so the obstruction would need another condition (e.g. 2 is a quartic residue, p = x² + 64y²).
why: Concrete, testable hypothesis class for the exceptions.
first_step: Compute for the four exceptions whether 2 is a quartic residue (p = x² + 64y²?) and whether −1 is an octic residue (p ≡ 1 mod 16?); compare to the frequency of these among non-exceptional primes ≡ 1 mod 8 below 20000.

title: Identity families indexed by other binary forms representing p: p = u² + 2v², u² + 3v², u² − 2v², u² + uv + v²
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 24 is simultaneously u² + v², u² + 2v² (p ≡ 1,3 mod 8 ✓), u² + 3v² (p ≡ 1 mod 3 ✓), u² − 2v² (p ≡ ±1 mod 8 ✓), u² + 6v²? (needs p ≡ 1, 7 mod 24 ✓!). Each representation gives 2 parameters; polynomial identities in those parameters are not excluded by Mordell–Schinzel.
why: Multiplies the search space of 'legal' identity classes by the number of forms; the combination 'p = u² + 6v²' is special to the hard class p ≡ 1 mod 24.
first_step: Same Gröbner/ansatz search for each form; for p = u² + 6v² in particular (since 24 | 840 structure).
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Class number of ℚ(√−p) and ES: correlation test
connection: h(−4p) controls representations of p by binary forms of discriminant −4p ↔ ES solutions involve binary forms 4uB·…
why: If R(p) correlates with h(−4p) or h(4p)·log ε_p, a class-number formula identity might lurk.
first_step: Compute Pearson/Spearman correlation of R(p)/log²p with h(−4p)/√p and with L(1, χ_p) over primes ≤ 10⁷.

title: Pell equations and ES: x² − D y² = ±4p via units
connection: Representations of 4p or p by norm forms of real quadratic fields always exist when the class group is trivial ↔ ES certificates as norms.
why: Norm-form existence is pointwise (class field theory: p splits ⟹ represented by some form in class group). ES would need a norm-form whose class group is trivial and whose representation yields a certificate.
first_step: Look for D (fixed, small) with h(D) = 1 such that every representation p = N(α) produces an ES certificate via an explicit formula; test D = 5, 8, 12, 13.

title: Quaternion / sums of four squares representations: many representations (r₄(p) = 8(p+1)) as thick object
connection: p = a²+b²+c²+d² has 8(p+1) representations — a thick object at p ↔ certificate extraction from some representation.
why: Thick object × extraction rule (G1): we need a rule mapping some 4-square representation to an ES certificate; the thick set has size ≍ p, so a rule with success probability ≫ 1/p per rep suffices.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, enumerate four-square representations and test simple formulas (e.g. x = (a²+b²)·k...) for producing certificates; record any rule with high success.

title: Three squares: p = a² + b² + c² representations (r₃ ≍ √p h) as thick object
connection: Odd p ≢ 7 mod 8 are sums of three squares with ≍ √p·L(1,χ) reps ↔ extraction rule to ES certificate.
why: Same G1 logic with an object of size √p tied to class numbers.
first_step: For hard p, enumerate three-square reps and search for any polynomial map (a,b,c) ↦ (x,y,z) yielding certificates on ≥ 1 rep for all p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Cohen–Lenstra heuristics for 'class gate' events
connection: Probability a random abelian group has given structure ↔ (ℤ/4C)^× subgroup generated by divisor classes containing −1.
why: Mostly a modelling tool; could predict which C slices fail more often (those with large 2-rank of (ℤ/4C)^×).
first_step: Compute slice failure rate vs 2-rank of (ℤ/4C)^× for C ≤ 200 over many p.

title: Quadratic reciprocity orientation: F_q is about (q/p); flip to (p/q) and use CRT-based identities
connection: (q/p) = (p/q) for p ≡ 1 mod 4 ↔ F_q becomes a condition on p mod q: p is a QNR mod q ⟹ ES(p). That's a residue-class condition mod q — so F_q is a finite covering statement mod q!
why: Since hard primes are ≡ 1 mod 4, F_q is a union of (q−1)/2 residue classes mod q; Mordell-style identities on these classes would prove F_q — but repo says F₁₁ open with a sterile point; so the classes are not covered by ET identities mod 11·(…). Check sterile point mechanism.
first_step: Read EXSET_CHAR_FORCING.md §7 on x** and determine which QNR classes mod 11 lack an ET identity at all moduli 11·M.

title: Dessins d'enfants / Belyi maps: the ES surface's fibration branched over 3 points?
connection: If the map (x,y,z) ↦ n restricted to some curve is a Belyi map, Galois action on dessins might act on ES solution structure.
why: Speculative; Belyi maps tie combinatorics to Galois action.
first_step: Check whether the map from the curve {y = z} on ES surfaces to the n-line is branched over ≤ 3 points.

title: Kernel-method / Gaussian process regression for R(p)/M(p) with arithmetic kernels
connection: Kernels k(p,q) based on shared residues (e.g. Σ_m w_m 1[p ≡ q mod m]) ↔ GP regression predicts R(p).
why: Learned kernel weights w_m identify the moduli that carry structure; residual variance quantifies randomness.
first_step: Fit a GP with arithmetic kernel on 10⁴ primes; inspect learned w_m.

title: Popoviciu's formula: N(n; a,b) = n/(ab) − {b′n/a} − {a′n/b} + 1 turns (★) into a sawtooth extremality condition
connection: Popoviciu: number of representations of n by ⟨a,b⟩ in terms of fractional parts with a′ ≡ a⁻¹ (mod b), b′ ≡ b⁻¹ (mod a) ↔ n is a k-Frobenius number iff both fractional parts take their maximum (a−1)/a, (b−1)/b, i.e. n ≡ −b (mod a) and n ≡ −a (mod b) (the pair form).
why: Links ES to sawtooth functions ((x)) and hence Dedekind sums and Dedekind/Rademacher reciprocity — reciprocity laws are exactly where T1-type parity information lives (repo's Dedekind–HJ charge was χ-blind; this is a different Dedekind-sum entry point via semigroup counting).
first_step: Write Σ over (u,B) of the Popoviciu sawtooth product for fixed p and check whether summing with weights yields a Dedekind-sum expression with a reciprocity-law evaluation.

title: Euler-type prime-generating polynomials as thin families (n² + n + 41 and relatives)
connection: Values of n² + n + 41 are prime for n ≤ 39; families with high prime density concentrate primes with special splitting (class number 1 field ℚ(√−163)) ↔ a thin family with rigid arithmetic.
why: Rigid splitting (every small prime is inert in ℚ(√−163)) is exactly the 'all small q are QNR-like' structure that affects F_q forcing lines; checking R on this family probes that interaction.
first_step: Compute R(p)/M_BM(p) for primes p = n² + n + 41 ≡ 1 mod 4 (n ≤ 10⁵) vs random primes.

title: Heath-Brown's density of integers with two-square prime factors
connection: A density theorem uses quadratic-form factorization to force prime factors of a special type (F05w,F29,F31), matching ES's Gaussian-integer hard case and character-sum averages (F20).
why: It demonstrates how Gaussian factorization can turn average arithmetic information into many explicit witnesses, potentially enriching ES's p≡1 mod 4 analysis.
first_step: Check Heath-Brown's exact two-square-prime-factor result and test its Gaussian-integer decomposition on 4Cp+1.
refs: unverified: Heath-Brown, The divisor function at values of a quadratic polynomial (1980s); source/title to verify

title: Universal quadratic form escalation as an ES covering strategy
connection: The 290 proof escalates from local representation data to a universal form, while ES combines a finite congruence cover with parametrized certificate families (F03,F09,F34).
why: An escalation analogue might iteratively enlarge certificate families whenever an uncovered residue class remains, providing a disciplined alternative to guessing isolated identities.
first_step: Translate each ES certificate line into a representation vector and simulate escalation on residue classes modulo 840, tracking which new line covers each uncovered class.

title: Spinor-genus representation obstruction with congruence conditions
connection: The ternary quadratic-form and lattice-coset spinor-genus classification in arXiv:2104.08798 matches ES F31/F29/F03 and F21: a representation problem with congruence-restricted integral vectors can have exceptional classes.
why: It supplies a precise quadratic-form framework relevant to ES's Gaussian/quadratic-form reformulations and residue-class restrictions.

alt_first_steps: [signature-0173] Compare the exceptional square classes from the ES Mordell-Schinzel discussion against spinor-exception shapes in this paper's classification.

title: Ternary lattice-coset representation versus ES three denominators
connection: Arxiv:2104.08798 treats ternary integral quadratic forms with congruence conditions, matching ES F12/F27/F31 and F03: three variables, positivity/integrality constraints, and congruence-restricted representations.
why: A ternary-form reduction could convert ES into a standard representation problem with mature local and spinor-genus tools.
first_step: Attempt the encoding for p≡1 mod 4 and verify whether the congruence conditions define a fixed lattice coset amenable to spinor-genus tests.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0205] Attempt to eliminate one ES denominator using a fixed slice and identify whether the remaining condition is a ternary quadratic form on a fixed coset.

title: Quadratic-form representations through continuants
connection: Arxiv:1203.0347 extends H. J. S. Smith's continuant approach to proper binary quadratic-form representations and gives deterministic algorithms; this matches ES F16/F17/F31 and F32.
why: ES's negative-continuant and continued-fraction formulations invite a constructive bridge from continuant identities to integral representations.
first_step: Take p≡1 mod 4, compute its two-square representation using the paper's algorithm, and inspect whether the output naturally supplies ES denominator congruences.

title: Least nonresidue bounds as a reciprocity-search analogue
connection: The Fourier-optimization bounds for least quadratic nonresidues in arXiv:2404.08380 match ES F08/F29/F36 and F21: a pointwise quadratic-character condition is central, but conditional distribution bounds do not automatically solve a single-integer witness problem.
why: The technique is a specific character-sum optimization tool to compare with ES's reciprocity obstruction at squares.
first_step: Read the Fourier optimization setup and test whether its majorant/minorant can bound the number of ES parameters excluded by the relevant quadratic character.

title: Hasse norm principle and norm-form equations
connection: Norm-form local-global problems share F06, F07, F20, F29; quadratic characters encode splitting and local constraints.
why: A norm-form reparametrisation could clarify the role of Gaussian splitting without assuming a new obstruction exists.
first_step: Rewrite the hard p≡1 mod 4 case using norms from Q(i), then compare local-global criteria for the resulting norm equation.

title: Pell equations and thin prime families
connection: Pell-type problems share F02w, F30, F34, often proving infinite but thin parameterized families.
why: A family of ES-valid primes could serve as a rung in a covering system, even without positive density.
first_step: Search Pell parameterisations yielding ES identities and compute the induced prime residue classes symbolically.

title: Quadratic reciprocity obstructions in parametrised identities
connection: Reciprocity-limited parametrisations share F08, F09, F29: a natural family fails on a quadratic-residue locus.
why: Alternative reciprocity symbols or multiple parameters may cover complementary loci.
first_step: For each known ES family, record its Legendre-symbol condition and test whether two families have complementary failure sets.

title: Branching of prime representations by quadratic forms
connection: Quadratic-form representation problems share F29, F31, F36 and encode prime classes through splitting and lattice points.
why: Representation by several related forms might give complementary prime classes analogous to a family-cover strategy.
first_step: List the quadratic forms in ES reformulations and compare their represented prime classes via genus characters.

title: Zhi-Wei Sun's family of refined-Lagrange conjectures with explicit finite exception lists
connection: Sun posed dozens of 'every n is … with constraint …' conjectures, each with finite explicit exceptions; several were proved (ternary forms, quaternions, spinor theory). Shares F01, F25, F23.
why: A large catalogue of solved siblings sharing the 'finite explicit exceptions' feature (like U(n)) with documented proof techniques.

title: Feature flip F31: Gauss's three-squares count r₃(n) ~ class number — a lattice count with a class-number main term
connection: r₃(n) = 12h(−4n)-type formulas give pointwise lower bounds via Siegel. If any ES count is (even partially) a class number, Siegel-type lower bounds apply (ineffectively).
why: Search for a lattice/genus formulation where an ES sub-count equals a class number or a sum of class numbers of discriminants tied to p.
first_step: Compute R(p) and Σ_{small D} h(−Dp) for hard primes ≤ 10⁶ and regress; any exact relation would be striking.

title: Heath-Brown x³+2y³ cubic parity breaking analogue for norm-form certificates
connection: Heath-Brown's primes of the form x³+2y³ use a Type II estimate on a cubic norm form; ES certificates can be written as divisors of norms from Q(√−d) at fixed p.

first_step: Write the Type I certificate as: an ideal 𝔞 | (p + 2c√−d) with N𝔞 ≡ −p mod 4cd, i.e. a ray-class condition, and list the ray class field.
refs: Heath-Brown, Primes represented by x^3+2y^3, Acta Math. 186 (2001)

title: Maynard 'primes represented by incomplete norm forms' for ES norm forms
connection: Maynard (Forum Pi 2020) counts primes as norms N(a1ω1+…+akωk) with missing coordinates, using a sieve beyond classical parity; ES Type I divisor event is a norm-divisibility event in quadratic fields.
why: Incomplete-norm-form technology handles thin sets of algebraic integers, relevant to certificates where only a few coordinates vary (c,d at fixed p).
first_step: Check whether 'N𝔞 for 𝔞 | (p+2c√−d)' with c,d in boxes is an incomplete-norm-form set in Maynard's sense.

title: Browning–Matthiesen norm forms equal to products of linear polynomials
connection: BM prove HP/weak approximation for N_{K/ℚ}(x) = ∏ L_i(t) using additive combinatorics (GT linear equations machinery); ES Type I reads f | N(p + 2c√−d) — divisors of norms of linear forms in (c,d).

first_step: Rewrite the Type I event as the solubility of N_{ℚ(√−d)/ℚ}(α) = f·g with α linear in parameters and match to BM's setting.
refs: Browning–Matthiesen, Norm forms for arbitrary number fields as products of linear polynomials, Ann. Sci. ENS 50 (2017), arXiv:1307.7641

title: Lawrence–Venkatesh p-adic period maps for families of ES curves
connection: LV prove finiteness of S-integral points on hypersurfaces/curves via big monodromy of p-adic period maps; ES Type I/II fibres (fix one denominator) are genus-0 curves, but auxiliary curves (fix two certificate parameters with extra integrality) may have higher genus.

refs: Lawrence–Venkatesh, Diophantine problems and p-adic period mappings, Invent. Math. 221 (2020), arXiv:1807.02721

title: S-unit equation finiteness: ES solutions with all denominators S-smooth
connection: If x, y, z, n are all S-units for a fixed finite set S, then 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is an S-unit equation with finitely many non-degenerate solutions (Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt).
why: Gives a rigorous negative: no fixed finite set of primes can supply the denominators for infinitely many primes n — a clean barrier for 'smooth-denominator' constructions.
first_step: Write the S-unit equation and its explicit Evertse bound; compare with the data on smoothness of ES denominators at p ≤ 10^7.
refs: Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt, Linear equations in variables which lie in a multiplicative group, Ann. Math. 155 (2002)

title: Chabauty–Kim / quadratic Chabauty on ES-derived S-unit curves
connection: Chabauty–Kim computes integral points on P¹ − {0,1,∞} (S-unit equations) and higher-genus curves (Balakrishnan–Dogra–Müller–Tuitman–Vonk); ES-derived S-unit curves appear when two denominators are constrained to be S-units.
why: Explicit computation of the finitely many exceptions would turn the S-unit barrier into data.
first_step: For S = {2,3,5,7}, compute all solutions of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z with x,y,z,n S-units by brute force / known S-unit solvers.
refs: Balakrishnan–Dogra–Müller–Tuitman–Vonk, Explicit Chabauty–Kim for the split Cartan modular curve of level 13, Ann. Math. 189 (2019)

title: Bhargava–Gauss composition of x²+4dy² values in Type I
connection: Type I needs f | p² + 4c²d: values of the form X² + 4dY² at (p,c); divisors of represented values are represented by forms in the same genus/class group (composition).
